source_text: καὶ ἕκαστος εἰς τὴν πατριὰν αὐτοῦ ἀπελεύσεσθε. Ἀφέσεως σημασία αὕτη, τὸ ἔτος τὸ πεντηκοστὸν ἐνιαυτὸς ἔσται ὑμῖν.» Τίς μὲν οὖν ὁ λόγος τοῦ καὶ αὐτὴν ἀνεῖσθαι τὴν γῆν, τί δὲ δὴ οὖν καὶ τὸ τῆς ἀφέσεως ἔτος ὑποδηλοῖ, βασανιοῦμεν εὐκαίρως· ὅτι δὲ ἐξαίρετος τοῖς Λευΐταις ὁ κλῆρος, λελέξεται· τέως δὲ γράφει ὡδὶ πάλιν· «Ἐὰν δέ τις ἀποδῶται τὴν οἰκίαν οἰκέτῃ τὴν ἐν πόλει τετειχισμένῃ, καὶ ἔσται ἡ λύτρωσις αὐτῆς, ἕως πληρωθῇ ἐνιαυτὸς ἡμερῶν, ἔσται ἡ λύτρωσις αὐτῆς· ἐὰν δὲ μὴ λυτρωθῇ, ἕως ἂν πληρωθῇ αὐτῆς ἐνιαυτὸς ὅλος, κυρωθήσεται ἡ οἰκία ἡ οὖσα ἐν πόλει τῇ ἐχούσῃ τεῖχος βεβαίως τῷ κτησαμένῳ αὐτὴν εἰς τὰς γενεὰς αὐτοῦ· καὶ οὐκ ἐξελεύσεται ἐν τῇ ἀφέσει. Αἱ δὲ οἰκίαι αἱ ἐν ἐπαύλεσιν, αἷς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν αὐταῖς τεῖχος κύκλῳ, πρὸς τὸν ἀγρὸν τῆς γῆς λογισθήσονται· λυτρωταὶ διαπαντὸς ἔσονται, καὶ ἐν τῇ ἀφέσει ἐξελεύσονται. Καὶ αἱ πόλεις τῶν Λευϊτῶν, οἰκίαι τῶν πόλεων κατασχέσεως αὐτῶν, λυτρωταὶ διαπαντὸς ἔσονται τοῖς Λευΐταις, καὶ ὃς ἂν λυτρώσηται παρὰ τῶν Λευϊτῶν, καὶ ἐξελεύσεται ἡ διάπρασις αὐτῶν οἰκιῶν πόλεως κατασχέσεως αὐτῶν ἐν τῇ ἀφέσει· ὅτι οἰκίαι τῶν πόλεων τῶν Λευϊτῶν κατάσχεσις αὐτῶν ἐν μέσῳ υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ, καὶ οἱ ἀγροὶ ἀφωρισμένοι ταῖς πόλεσιν αὐτῶν οὐ πραθήσονται· ὅτι κατάσχεσις αἰωνία τοῦτο αὐτῶν ἐστιν.» {ΠΑΛΛ.} Καὶ τί δὴ ἄρα φησὶν ὁ νόμος; συνίημι γὰρ οὐ σφόδρα. {ΚΥΡ.} Ἄκουε δή· τὰ μὲν γὰρ ἐν ἄστει τῶν οἰκοδομημάτων ἃ ἂν ἐκπρίαιντό τινες παρὰ τῶν κυρίων, ἐξέστω, φησὶ, τοῖς ἀποδομένοις, ἀναμοιράσασθαι τὸ δοθὲν καὶ μέχρις ἔτους ἑνός· εἰ δὲ μὴ τοῦτο γένηται, παρῳχηκότος ἐνιαυτοῦ, κύριος ἔστω, φησὶ, καὶ γραμμάτων ἔξω λοιπὸν ὁ πριάμενος. Εἰ δὲ ἀγρὸς εἴη καὶ ἔπαυλις, ἐξέστω, φησὶ, τὸ ἀνακομίζεσθαι διὰ παντὸς, ἐκτετικότος τῷ πριαμένῳ τὸ δοθὲν ἀργύριον τοῦ ἀπεμπωληκότος. Οὐκ ἔχοντος δὲ καταθεῖναι καὶ ἀναλαβεῖν, ἀνεῖσθαι προστέταχεν ἐν ἔτει πεντηκοστῷ, ἐκτετικότος οὐδὲν τοῦ πάλαι Κυρίου. Κατελογίζετο γὰρ ὁ νόμος τῷ πριαμένῳ τὴν κτῆσιν, τοῦ μακροῦ χρόνου τὰ κέρδη πρὸς τὴν τῶν ὀφλημάτων ἀντέκτισιν. Ἀλλὰ ταυτὶ μὲν ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀγελαίοις ἐθεσμοθέτει Θεός. Ἀνὰ μέρος δὲ ὥσπερ πάλιν καὶ ὡς ἐν ἰδίᾳ ἐτίθει τιμῇ τὰ Λευϊτικὰ, λυτρωτὰ διὰ παντὸς εἶναι λέγων αὐτὰ, καὶ ἐπιπράσκεσθαι διακωλύων· «Μερὶς γὰρ αὕτη, φησὶ, καὶ κλῆρος αὐτοῖς.» {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ἆρ' οὖν, ὦ γενναῖε, μέχρι τούτων ἡμῖν ὁ τοῦ νόμου σκοπὸς, ἐκτέκοι δ' ἂν ὅλως οὐδὲν τῶν ἀναγκαίων ἡ βάσανος; {ΚΥΡ.} Εἶτα πῶς πνευματικὸς ἔτι ὁ νόμος; ἢ πῶς οὐκ ἄξιον ἐννοεῖν, ὅ τί ποτε ἄρα φησὶ τὸ Γράμμα τὸ ἱερὸν, τοῦ δὴ χάριν, ἀλύτρωτα μὲν τὰ ἐν ἄστει παρῳχηκότος ἐνιαυτοῦ ἑνὸς, ἐλλυτρώσιμα δὲ καὶ διὰ παντὸς τὰ ἔξω καὶ ἐν ἀγροῖς; Ἀλλ' ἔστιν ἰδεῖν ὡς οὐ σφόδρα πολὺς τῷ πανσόφῳ Θεῷ τῆς ἱστορίας ὁ λόγος, ἔστ' ἂν ἴοι καταροῦν τὰ πνευματικὰ, καὶ τῆς ἀληθείας οἱ χαρακτῆρες ἀκριβεῖς λίαν ἐκφαίνοιντο.
pass_a_gloss: [Lev 25:10–11 continued:] '...and each to his family/clan you will go away. This signal of release, the fiftieth year, will be a year for you.' What then is the reason for the land itself also being released, and what the year of release hints, we will examine at a fitting time; but that the lot is select for the Levites will be said; meanwhile he writes thus again: 'If someone sells the house [printed: to a servant,; LXX: dwelling, ] in a walled city, its redemption will also be, until a year of days is fulfilled; its redemption will be; but if it is not redeemed until its whole year is fulfilled, the house in the city that has a wall will be confirmed securely to the one who acquired it, to his generations; and it will not go out in the release. But the houses in villages/farmsteads, which have no wall round about, will be reckoned toward the field of the land; they will be redeemable always, and they will go out in the release. And the cities of the Levites, houses of the cities of their possession, will be redeemable always for the Levites; and whoever redeems from the Levites, the sale of their houses of the city of their possession will also go out in the release; because the houses of the cities of the Levites are their possession in the midst of the sons of Israel, and the fields set apart for their cities will not be sold, because this is their eternal possession.' PALL: And what then does the law say? For I do not understand very much. CYR: Hear then: the buildings in a town which some might buy from the owners, let it be permitted, it says, to those who sold to give back/re divide what was given, up to one year; but if this does not happen, the year having passed, let the buyer be owner, it says, and henceforth outside documents/written terms. But if it be a field and a farmstead, let recovery be permitted always, the seller having paid back to the buyer the silver given; but if he does not have [it] to deposit and take back, he ordered it to be released in the fiftieth year, the former owner paying nothing. For the law reckoned to the buyer of the property the gains of the long time toward repayment of the debts. But these things God legislated for the common folk. But separately, as it were, again and as in a special honor, he placed the Levitical things, saying they are redeemable always and preventing them from being sold: 'For this, he says, is their portion and lot.' PALL: Is then, noble one, the aim of the law up to these things for us, and would the testing/examination bring forth nothing at all of the necessary things? CYR: Then how is the law still spiritual? Or how is it not worthy to consider whatever the sacred Writing says, for what reason the things in town are unredeemable after one year has passed, but redeemable always those outside and in fields? But one can see that the account of the history is not very great to the all wise God, as long as he might go on to plow up the spiritual things, and the impressions/features of the truth be shown forth very exactly.
pass_b_english: Cyril: …and each of you shall return to his family. This is a jubilee of release; the fiftieth year shall be a year for you’ (Leviticus 25:10–11). Why even the land itself is released, and what the year of release signifies, we shall examine at the proper time. That the Levites’ lot is a special one will be shown; for the present, he writes again as follows: ‘If anyone sells a dwelling house in a walled city, it may be redeemed until a full year of days is completed; there shall be redemption for it. But if it is not redeemed before its whole year is completed, the house that is in the city that has a wall shall be confirmed securely to the one who bought it, for his generations, and it shall not go out in the release. But the houses in villages that have no wall around them shall be reckoned as the field of the land; they shall always be redeemable, and they shall go out in the release. And the cities of the Levites, the houses of the cities of their possession, shall always be redeemable for the Levites. And if anyone redeems from the Levites, the sale of their houses in the city of their possession shall also go out in the release; for the houses of the cities of the Levites are their possession in the midst of the sons of Israel, and the fields set apart for their cities shall not be sold, for this is their everlasting possession’ (Leviticus 25:29–34).
Palladius: And what, then, does the law mean? For I do not quite understand.

Cyril: Listen, then. When people buy buildings in a town from their owners, the sellers, it says, may refund what they were given, for up to one year. If this does not happen, then once the year has passed, let the buyer be the owner, it says, and from then on beyond any written claim. But if it is a field and a farmstead, let it be allowed, it says, to recover it at any time, once the one who sold it has paid back to the buyer the money he was given. If he cannot pay it back and recover the property, the law commanded that it be released in the fiftieth year, without the former owner paying anything. For the law credited the buyer of the property with the profits of the long period as repayment of what was owed. These things God laid down for the common people. But the Levites’ holdings he set apart once more, as it were, in an honor of their own, saying that they are redeemable at all times and forbidding them to be sold: ‘For this,’ it says, ‘is their portion and lot’ (Leviticus 25:34).
Palladius: Then does the aim of the law go no further than this for us, my noble friend, and would close examination yield nothing at all that we need?

Cyril: Then how is the law still spiritual (Romans 7:14)? Or how is it not worth considering what the sacred Scripture means, and for what reason houses in a town cannot be redeemed once one year has passed, while those outside, in the fields, can be redeemed at any time? But one can see that the all-wise God gives no great weight to the history, so long as the spiritual meaning runs smoothly on its course and the features of the truth shine out with great exactness.

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of De adoratione Book 13 to compare. Sense taken from the PG 68 Greek. The withheld earlier English was not used as a model.

apparatus.note: Section opens mid-quotation (Leviticus 25:10, begun at the end of section 12). Leviticus 25:29: the Migne text prints τὴν οἰκίαν οἰκέτῃ ('the house to a servant'), which makes no sense in context and is almost certainly a corruption of the LXX οἰκίαν οἰκητήν ('a dwelling house'); translated as 'a dwelling house'. Doubtful reading flagged for review. Leviticus 25:29 LXX repeats 'its redemption shall be' (ἔσται ἡ λύτρωσις αὐτῆς); rendered 'it may be redeemed... there shall be redemption for it'. Leviticus 25:33 (ὃς ἂν λυτρώσηται παρὰ τῶν Λευϊτῶν) is obscure in the LXX as in the Hebrew; rendered with Brenton's sense ('if anyone redeems from the Levites'). In Cyril's paraphrase, ἀναμοιράσασθαι τὸ δοθέν is taken as 'refund what was given' (that is, undo the sale by repaying the price); γραμμάτων ἔξω ('outside the writings') is taken as 'beyond any written claim' (the sale becomes final); both renderings are uncertain. ὁ πάλαι κύριος is the former owner (κύριος here means owner, not the Lord, despite the capital in the print). The quoted phrase 'For this is their portion and lot' is not an exact verse: it summarizes Leviticus 25:34 ('this is their everlasting possession') in the language of Numbers 18:20 and Deuteronomy 10:9; cited to Leviticus 25:34. Romans 7:14 cited for 'the law is spiritual' (ὁ νόμος πνευματικός ἐστιν). Reviewer: the print's καταροῦν is read as κατὰ ῥοῦν ('with the stream, smoothly', a common idiom with ἰέναι), run together in the print. The grammar requires it: singular ἴοι takes the neuter plural τὰ πνευματικά as subject, beside plural ἐκφαίνοιντο with masculine οἱ χαρακτῆρες; the earlier reading 'God goes on to plow up the spiritual things' (καταρόω) leaves τὰ πνευματικά without a construction parallel to the second clause. 'So long as' for ἔστ' ἂν with the optative follows the sense. Emendation, not a manuscript reading.
